column5: lights for appointed times
column6: The commentary says qaddara includes the amount and timing assigned to each thing; Genesis gives the sun and moon their signs, seasons, days and years, making timekeeping part of creation's order.

column5: creatures according to their kinds
column6: The commentary says its objectless measure and guidance extend to every being; Genesis has the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds, showing the varied forms within that universal scope.

column5: nations allotted with fixed boundaries
column6: The commentary says qaddara determines how far each thing reaches; in WLC's wording, Moses says the Most High apportioned nations and fixed their boundaries according to the number of Israel's children, extending measured allotment to peoples.

column5: sun runs its appointed course
column6: The commentary connects measured celestial paths with time and travel; the psalm compares the sun to a runner that rejoices to complete its course, giving the solar route a vivid motion.

column5: sun's circuit reaches the ends of heaven
column6: The commentary says a measured thing has a course with an endpoint; the psalm says the sun rises at one end of heaven and its circuit reaches the other, adding the full extent of its route.

column5: God measures the earth
column6: The commentary says measure establishes the reach and limit of created things; Habakkuk portrays God standing and measuring the earth before nations tremble, making measurement an act of sovereign judgment over the land.

column5: God changes times and seasons
column6: The commentary says a thing's measure includes its term and timing; Daniel blesses God as the one who changes times and seasons and raises or removes kings, extending providential ordering to political history.

column5: God declares the end from the beginning
column6: The commentary defines a thing's measure by its reach, essence and end; Isaiah says God declares the end from the beginning and accomplishes his purpose, making the endpoint part of divine intention.

column5: each thing made for its purpose and day
column6: The commentary says measure gives each thing where it will arrive and end; Proverbs says the Lord made everything for its purpose, including the wicked for a day of trouble, specifying purpose and endpoint.

column5: just scales belong to the Lord
column6: The commentary says human weighing must follow the measure God gives; Proverbs says honest scales and weights are the Lord's work, grounding fair human measurement in divine order.

column5: no injustice in measures and weights
column6: The commentary connects divine measure to the human use of a scale; Leviticus forbids injustice in length, weight or capacity, turning measure into a concrete command for commerce.

column5: true weights and measures required
column6: The commentary says people may measure but must honor a measure they did not invent; Leviticus requires honest balances, weights, ephah and hin, giving that limit a practical legal form.

column5: God makes the paths straight
column6: The commentary says the guide both shows a route and leads toward its destination; Proverbs tells the hearer to acknowledge God in all ways so that God will make the paths straight.

column5: God weighs the spirit behind human ways
column6: The commentary says a person's self-measure may be mistaken; Proverbs says people may see their own ways as pure while the Lord weighs their spirits, placing judgment of inward motives with God.

column5: nations learn God's ways and walk in them
column6: The commentary describes a guide who shows a way that followers then take; Isaiah pictures nations going to God's mountain to be taught his ways and walk in his paths, joining instruction to following.

column5: God teaches the way with his eye upon the learner
column6: The commentary says a guide accompanies and identifies the route, not merely pointing from afar; the psalm promises instruction in the way to go and counsel with God's eye upon the person.

column5: God establishes a person's steps
column6: The commentary distinguishes the guide's action from the walker's progress; the psalm says a person's steps are established by the Lord and that the Lord upholds him when he falls, joining direction to support.

column5: steps made firm by God's word
column6: The commentary says the path shown by God must be followed by the traveler; the psalm asks God to make the speaker's steps firm by his word and not let iniquity rule him, making guidance practical and ethical.

column5: righteous path grows brighter
column6: The commentary says the same road is taken by some and avoided by others; Proverbs compares the righteous path to dawn growing brighter, depicting one response as progress toward full light.

column5: wicked path is darkness and stumbling
column6: The commentary says another person turns aside from the shown way; Proverbs describes the wicked person's path as darkness in which he cannot see what makes him stumble, giving the rejected way its own consequence.

column5: snow and frost given by God
column6: The commentary presents weather and vegetation as parts of a measured natural course; the psalm says God gives snow like wool and scatters frost like ashes, adding cold season to the ordering of rain and grass.

column5: God's word melts ice and releases water
column6: The commentary reads growth and decay as stages in one course; the psalm says God sends his word, melts the ice and makes waters flow, showing the natural transition from cold to movement.

column5: the farmer places different seeds in order
column6: The commentary says qaddara can mean preparing something to fit its use; Isaiah's farmer sows different grains in their proper places, showing practical measure in cultivation.

column5: God teaches the farmer his craft
column6: The commentary says preparation and measure are first God's work and then human work under a given measure; Isaiah says God instructs the farmer in the right way to proceed, presenting ordinary skill as taught by God.

column5: Rebekah follows the servant toward Isaac
column6: The commentary notes the concrete sense of escorting a bride to her husband; Genesis says Rebekah and her attendants follow Abraham's servant on the journey, making the bride's movement toward her marriage an enacted image of being led.

column5: Isaac receives Rebekah as his wife
column6: The commentary says the bride's guidance has a destination in the husband's home; Genesis ends the journey with Isaac taking Rebekah as his wife, naming the arrival that completes the escort.

column5: ark leads on a way Israel has not traveled
column6: The commentary says a guide goes ahead and makes an unknown route knowable; Joshua tells Israel to follow the ark at a distance so they will know the way, because they have not passed that way before.

column5: light guides feet into the way of peace
column6: The commentary connects light, a traveler's feet and the path to a destination; Zechariah says the dawn from on high will shine on those in darkness and guide their feet into the way of peace.

column5: Abraham departs without knowing the destination
column6: The commentary presents Abraham's trust that God will guide him on the road ahead; Hebrews says Abraham obeyed the call and went out without knowing where he was going, making that trust a journey into an unknown future.

column5: a messenger sent ahead to prepare the way
column6: The commentary says a guide is named for going in front of the traveler; Mark introduces the messenger sent ahead to prepare the Lord's way, giving that image a prophetic and communal role.

column5: voice prepares a straight road in the wilderness
column6: The commentary links the way shown with the route the traveler must take; Mark's wilderness voice calls for the Lord's road to be prepared and made straight, turning guidance into communal preparation.

column5: Wisdom will guide and guard the speaker
column6: The commentary says God's guidance can become a personal, continuing relationship; Solomon asks for Wisdom to accompany him, guide his actions and guard him, turning universal guidance into a prayer for daily direction.

column5: the king weighed and found wanting
column6: The commentary depicts a man measuring revelation by his own judgment and reaching a false verdict; Daniel interprets the writing against Belshazzar as God having weighed him and found him wanting, reversing who sets the measure.

column5: do not require bit and bridle
column6: The commentary says hidaya is gentle leading rather than forced dragging; the psalm warns the hearer not to be like a horse or mule that must be restrained with bit and bridle, making the contrast with coerced movement explicit.

column5: seasons judged for produce and water
column6: The commentary says rain, pasture and time are measured parts of one natural course; the Mishnah assigns judgments for produce, tree fruit and water to their appointed festivals, giving seasonal provision a Jewish calendar and liturgical frame.

column5: birth, life and death beyond one's control
column6: The commentary says each thing has an allotted term and endpoint; Avot says a person is born, lives and dies against his will and will give account, turning the measure of lifespan into a rabbinic reflection on agency.

column5: Jesus identifies himself as the way to the Father
column6: The commentary says guidance joins a route to the home it reaches; Jesus says he is the way and that no one comes to the Father except through him, making the destination personal in John's account.

column5: those led by God's Spirit are God's children
column6: The commentary says guidance is God's act while taking the way identifies the follower; Paul calls those led by God's Spirit children of God, making the response a mark of belonging.
